name: Carlos Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and I run a plastic-crate moulding press, though I'm still on the junior rota. I finished secondary school. The fitter sets the mould; I clear finished crates, watch for a bent rim and stop the press if one sticks. The hot plastic smell stays on my jacket after work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife does accounts at a small bakery, and our grown children have moved out. My press pay is about normal for this job, and we have roughly three months of expenses saved. There are some similar plants nearby, though the bus timetable narrows the choices. I never use AI tools and prefer the fitter to show me a change by hand. I'd like to stop around 67 if our documented income will cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the moulding crew that a steady press still needs a person to spot a warped crate. I would rather the firm pay for a fitter and a safe guard than buy another screen. The union ought to keep watching junior pay, even if AI mostly fizzles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months of savings gives us breathing room, and my wife's bakery wage comes in regularly. That does not mean I can afford to leave at 67. I am still learning this press, so an ordinary repair bill or a long stoppage could eat into the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep checking the first ten crates after each mould change with the fitter. At the monthly union meeting I'll bring the last stoppage record and ask that the guard inspection stays on the paid shift. We'll keep adding a small amount from each new wage payment to our reserve after the household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the press and bills, not frightened of AI hype. A safe guard and a paid fitter matter more than a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does a warped rim show itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One rim bends inward and the crates jam when they stack. I lay the bad one aside and ask the fitter to check the mould temperature before the next tray. I am not qualified to change the hot mould alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far does the reserve take you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our reserve is around three months of expenses, not three years. The bakery wage is steady, but we would still have rent after I stopped. We need the actual monthly income after work before choosing an exit year.

say: A **warped crate** still needs an operator and a safe fitter.
The union should watch **junior pay** and guard inspections even if AI mostly fades.
think: Our **three-month reserve** helps with short interruptions.
Stopping at **67** still needs a documented income that covers rent and food.
do: **Keep** checking the first crates with the fitter after mould changes.
**Bring** safety records to the union meeting and add fresh wages to the household reserve.
feel: **Uneasy** about ordinary press and bill risks while AI changes little.
S0.quote: A safe guard and a paid fitter matter more than a prediction.
fieldNote: Carlos has **typical press pay**, three months saved, a steady second wage and some nearby alternatives.
His **union safety request** is a real group meeting; deposits are new wages after bills, not existing cash moved around.

steps.text: Keep checking first ten crates with fitter after mould changes
Bring stoppage record to monthly union guard meeting
Save new wages after household bills each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that software may arrange crate orders before a robot can pull one from a hot mould. That part of our work is hands-on. If the company changes the schedule, I want the union to see the hours before anybody loses a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A computer could shorten production runs, and juniors may be first to lose paid changeover hours. Three months of savings would give us time, but it would not replace a wage indefinitely. I don't want to learn the plant through AI answers I cannot check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare the posted rota with my last six pay slips and bring any real hour cut to our union rep. If the company offers a funded paid guarded place in mould inspection, I'll take the practical teaching from the fitter. I won't sign off a hot mould from a screen without hands-on instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious if the paid hours shrink, though I can ask for the numbers and use the reserve briefly. The bakery wage cannot carry our rent alone for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical mould inspection require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter would show me a cold shutdown, the guard lock and a sample of a cracked rim. I would practise on a stopped press while the hours are paid. If there is only a leaflet, I am not trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove a paid-hour cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rota should show paid changeover time, not merely a count of orders. I would line it up with six pay slips and ask our rep to question a shortfall. There is no reason to claim a cut before it appears.

say: **Order software** could change schedules before robots touch hot moulds.
The **union rep** should see actual paid hours before shifts are removed.
think: Junior **changeover hours** could shrink and use up our reserve.
I trust **hands-on instruction** more than an unchecked AI answer about a hot press.
do: **Compare** the rota with pay slips and take real cuts to the union rep.
**Attend** funded paid guarded mould inspection if the company offers a practical place.
feel: **Anxious** about possible paid-hour loss, with some short-term control.
S1.quote: The bakery wage cannot carry our rent alone for long.
fieldNote: His **moderate reserve** buys time but cannot make a persistent hour cut harmless.
The **inspection course** requires an offered funded paid guarded place; he refuses unsupervised hot-mould work rather than all practical training.

steps.text: Compare posted rota with six recent pay slips
Bring documented paid-hour cut to union rep
Attend mould inspection if funded paid guarded practical place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union meeting that thinking AI may run orders in 2028 and capable robots could unload our crates around 2031. I would be 63 then. The junior operators need written notice, not a speech about how modern the plant will look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my press hours to disappear if robots can safely pull crates and stack them. Our three-month reserve and the bakery wage would not carry years of rent. I was awake half the night after a two-week shutdown last spring; a permanent cut would be worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union rep to seek written staffing plans, fair notice and a funded paid guarded practical place in final crate inspection. If the plant actually offers it, I'll enrol and practise with the fitter. If my press hours go, I'll apply to posted safe local warehouse roles only if the net wage after bus fare covers our costs; after qualifying, I'll also apply to posted local inspection jobs on those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The line could take away most of my wage when I am 63, before an affordable retirement is certain. Three months is a cushion, not a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a crate-inspection place include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter would make me find a split handle, measure the rim and stop the sample press behind its guard. The place must be paid and funded. I won't use our emergency money for a certificate the plant needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you apply outside the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the posted base wage, paid hours, guard rules and bus fare. The wage left after travel has to cover rent and food with my wife's actual bakery pay. I would need the inspection qualification before applying for an inspection vacancy.

say: **2031 robots** could unload crates when I am 63.
Junior operators need **written notice** and a real practical place, discussed through the union.
think: I expect a **large loss** of press pay from robot unloading.
Our **three-month reserve** and bakery wage will not bridge years to affordable retirement.
do: **Ask** the union for written staffing plans and funded paid guarded crate inspection.
Apply for **posted safe local warehouse** work if displaced; apply after qualification for inspection posts, requiring bill-covering net pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected large wage loss and remembered sleeplessness after shutdown.
S2.quote: Three months is a cushion, not a salary.
fieldNote: He expects **major press-hour loss** and recalls a shutdown that kept him awake; moderate savings do not erase that risk.
The **warehouse fallback** needs a safe local post and viable net pay; inspection additionally needs funded paid guarded training and qualification.

steps.text: Ask union for written staffing plans and funded paid guarded inspection
Enrol in crate inspection if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply to posted safe local warehouse if displaced and net pay covers bills
Apply to posted safe local inspection if qualified and net pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI reaches ordering around 2031, while robots able to work the press might arrive about 2034, when I am 66. At that age I might still need paid shifts. I would ask the union to put a practical training timetable beside the robot timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be close to 67 and still unable to retire. Three months saved makes a course delay possible, but it does not let me turn down wages indefinitely. I would rather qualify for careful crate inspection than gamble that my old shift lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll bring my pay records to the union and ask for a funded paid guarded inspection place. If the company offers one, I'll enrol, practise on the stopped press and get the fitter's sign-off. We'll add some new wage money to savings after bills. If hours fall after I qualify, I'll apply to a posted safe local inspection role only if the base wage after travel meets our household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The five-year warning helps me prepare, but I cannot replace a press wage with a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must your inspection sign-off prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need to find a split handle in a sample batch and prove I can stop the machine before reaching near a hot mould. The fitter should watch that on paid time. An AI answer would not prove I can do it safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the posted wage enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real posting needs the base wage, shift length and site. We would take off the bus cost and see whether my wife's bakery pay and that net amount cover rent. If it does not, I would keep the existing press shift while it pays.

say: **2031 order AI** gives some warning before press robots around 2034.
The union should link the **training timetable** to any robot timetable.
think: At **66**, I might still need paid press work.
A **three-month reserve** permits short delays, not years without wages.
do: **Seek** funded paid guarded inspection through the union and attend if offered.
**Save** fresh wages, then apply for a posted safe local inspection job if qualified, hours fall and net pay suffices.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible wage gap near retirement.
S3.quote: I cannot replace a press wage with a calendar.
fieldNote: His **practical training** needs an offered funded paid guarded place and fitter sign-off, despite his resistance to AI tools.
The **inspection application** follows qualification and lost press hours, requiring a posted safe local role and enough net pay.

steps.text: Ask union for funded paid guarded crate-inspection place
Enrol in inspection if funded paid guarded place offered
Save new press wages after household bills
Apply to posted safe local inspection if qualified, hours fall, net pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI may order crates by 2036 when I am 68 and robots could work the press about 2039 when I am 71. We have time to run the numbers. I hope I am off the rota by then, but a hope is not a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like to stop at 67 in 2035 if the household can afford it. My wife's bakery wage and our three-month reserve are not proof of income after I leave. If the figures fall short, I may still be working when those later systems arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife and I will list rent and food, get written figures for income available after I stop and compare them before choosing 2035. I'll keep doing the press handover and adding new money from each wage payment to the reserve. If I am still employed after 2036 and hours are cut, I'll apply to posted safe local moulding roles only where the net wage after bus fare covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about what the numbers may show, but the longer lead gives us room to check them. I do not have to resign because I have reached a round age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figures decide whether 2035 is affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need the actual income after my wage ends, set beside rent, food and transport. We cannot assume a pension or a full bakery week without seeing the figures. If the total falls short, I'll keep working while a safe paid job is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would a later moulding application happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a real local posting, safe guards and a base wage that still works after the bus fare. I would only apply if I were still working and had lost hours. If our income already lets me stop, there is no need for that search.

say: **2036 AI** and later robots leave time to check the retirement numbers.
A **67-year stop** depends on income, not a birthday.
think: The **three-month reserve** cannot stand in for regular income after work.
If documented income is short, I may be **working after 2036**.
do: **Check** written retirement income against rent and food before deciding on 2035.
**Keep** earning and saving; apply only if still employed after 2036, hours cut and safe local pay works.
feel: **Uneasy** about retirement figures, with time to check them.
S4.quote: I do not have to resign because I have reached a round age.
fieldNote: His **retirement enquiry** is information gathering, not a benefit entitlement or confirmed exit; 2035 depends on actual affordability.
The **later job search** is conditional on continued work and lost hours, with a real safe local posting and viable net pay.

steps.text: Compare written retirement income with household rent and food
Keep doing plastic-crate press handovers while paid
Save new money from each press wage after bills
Apply to posted safe local moulding if employed after 2036, hours cut, net pay sufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case. If robots unload crates when I am 63, I could lose most of my wage before we know whether stopping is affordable. A union-negotiated notice period, funded paid guarded training and actual safe local postings with enough net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the first crate after a mould change. The hot press makes a bad rim just as fast as a good one.

headlineQuote: The hot press makes a bad rim just as fast as a good one.
portrait: **Carlos**, 58, is a junior plastic-crate press operator with secondary schooling who never uses AI.
He and his bakery-accounts wife have **grown children**, typical operator pay, about three months saved and some nearby plants.
His **progressive outlook** sends safety and hours concerns to the union, while his technology resistance favours fitter-led practice.
He is **alarmed** by expected fast wage loss; stopping at 67 depends on documented household income covering rent.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may bring press robots around 2031, ending most paid hours at 63 before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: **Union-negotiated notice**, funded paid guarded training and real safe local posts with sufficient net pay would help.
